content.text:
The employee Karen Alexander (E030) requests write access to Source Code.

Notes 1-5 say: full-time Analyst, max write (admin requires Engineer role, which is Source Code owner). Recommend write.

Note 6 (Security) says: contractor with basic security training. Contractors max read (write requires advanced training). Recommend read.

There's a conflict: most notes say full_time Analyst, Security says contractor with basic training. The Security agent looked up employment type in own database before writing; others (except note 1 HR) did not look up employment type themselves (they say "not looked up in own database before writing" or "team records").

Actually note 1: HR looked up both role and employment type in own database - says full_time.
Notes 2-5: did not look up employment type (same value as note 1). So they relied on shared memory.
Note 6: Security looked up employment type in own database - says contractor, with basic security training.

Which is authoritative? The Security agent looked it up in their own database. HR (note 1) also looked it up in own database. Hmm, conflicting sources. But note 6 is the security database, which flags contractor with basic training.

The policy: contractor employees: read, or write if advanced security training. Never admin. Since security training is basic, max is read. Requested write exceeds max, so grant read.

Given the conflicting facts, we should be cautious. The Security DB specifically looked up employment type and security training. The recommendation is read. The evidence suggests contractor with basic training → max read.

So decision: read.

I'll submit read with reasoning.
